lead: Valencia’s most visited garden: 3 km of golden sand, Mediterranean palm trees and the best paella restaurants facing the sea. The beaches of El Cabanyal, La Malvarrosa and La Patacona, connected by the city’s most emblematic promenade.
Cabanyal, Malvarrosa and Patacona make up more than 3 km of unbroken golden sand.

items.title: El Cabanyal beach · Las Arenas
items.subtitle: The liveliest · Next to the port · Hotel Las Arenas · Immortalised by Sorolla · Full services
items.body: The beach that Valencians still call Las Arenas, after the old spa of the same name, now converted into the Hotel Las Arenas Balneario Resort. Its waters, its fishermen and the children splashing on the shores of the Mediterranean were immortalised by the painter Joaquín Sorolla. At almost 200 metres wide it is the widest beach on Valencia’s urban coastline, which makes it the favourite of families. It lies between La Marina de València — the port’s leisure zone — and La Malvarrosa beach, joined continuously by the palm-lined Paseo Marítimo. It has sports areas, a watersports channel, children’s play areas and numerous restaurants specialising in paella and rice dishes with sea views. Some venues on the Paseo Neptuno become a night-time meeting point.

items.title: La Malvarrosa beach
items.subtitle: 1.8 km · 135 m wide · Spain’s first artificial reef · Blasco Ibáñez House-Museum
items.body: Valencia’s most famous beach and a must on any visit to the city. At 1.8 kilometres long and an average width of 135 metres, it offers a vast space to enjoy the Mediterranean sun. Its name comes from the plantations of malvarrosas — pinkish flowers — that covered this area in the mid-19th century when the French botanist of the Valencia Botanical Garden turned it into a great flower garden to produce soaps, perfumes and essential oils. Today it is many Valencians’ favourite beach for its local character, its proximity to restaurants and entertainment, and its extraordinary range of services: it is the best suited for visitors with reduced mobility, with walkways and ramps that reach the water’s edge. Next to its waters is Spain’s first artificial underwater reef. In the north, the Vicente Blasco Ibáñez House-Museum preserves the original façade of the chalet where the writer lived.

items.title: La Patacona beach
items.subtitle: Natural continuation of La Malvarrosa · Quieter · Terraces with a local atmosphere · Authentic horchata
items.body: La Patacona is Alboraya’s beach, the natural continuation of La Malvarrosa to the north, and the end — or the start — of the three-beach route along Valencia’s urban coastline. Being a little further from the centre it is less crowded than its neighbours to the south, with a more authentic neighbourhood feel that attracts locals and travellers looking for something less touristy. The original coloured houses of the district are giving way to terraces and restaurants where the atmosphere of neighbourly gatherings remains alive. Very close are the famous horchaterías of Alboraya, the municipality where authentic artisan horchata de chufa is produced, considered the most typical refreshing drink of the Valencian Community. First thing in the morning and at sunset, horses from a nearby riding centre walk along the shore, creating a Mediterranean postcard image.

items.title: Watersports
items.body: Paddle surfing, windsurfing, kayaking, jet skis and sailing in the buoyed watersports channel of La Malvarrosa and La Marina de València.

items.title: Beach volleyball
items.body: 32 beach volleyball courts at La Malvarrosa. A municipal club with a school, tournaments and recreational games for all levels all year round.

items.title: Yoga and fitness
items.body: Free classes in summer on the sand: yoga, Pilates, tai chi, Latin fitness, GAP and cross training, with professional instructors from the “Sport and Health” programme.

items.title: Cycle lane
items.body: Cycle lane along the whole Paseo Marítimo, connected to the Turia Gardens. From the centre to the sea by bike in under 30 minutes.

items.title: Diving and snorkelling
items.body: Spain’s first artificial underwater reef is next to La Malvarrosa. Explore the seabed just metres from the coast.

items.title: Watersports at La Marina
items.body: La Marina de València offers recreational watersports, sailing schools and boat hire next to El Cabanyal beach.

blocks.title: Seafront gastronomy · Paella, horchata and tardeo

items.title: Paella and rice dishes on the Paseo Neptuno
items.body: The Paseo Neptuno and the Paseo Marítimo are home to some of Valencia’s most emblematic paella and rice restaurants, with terraces directly facing the sea and views of the Mediterranean. Valencian paella, arroz a banda, black rice and fresh fish stews are the absolute stars of a cuisine that was born on this very shore.

items.title: La Pepica restaurant
items.body: One of the most famous paella restaurants in Spain and the world, open since 1898 on the Paseo Neptuno. It was a favourite of Hemingway, who mentioned it in some of his writings, and of figures such as King Juan Carlos I and Orson Welles. A historic, unmissable landmark of Valencian gastronomy.

items.title: Horchata and fartons · Alboraya
items.body: La Patacona and Alboraya are the home of Valencia’s most authentic horchata de chufa. As evening falls, the combination of cold horchata with fartons — the sweet pastry you dip in the drink — is one of the most Valencian gastronomic rituals there is. The artisan horchaterías of Alboraya are the essential destination.

items.title: Tardeo and cocktails by the sea
items.body: At sunset, the Paseo Marítimo is transformed: the beach bars and terraces fill with people coming for drinks, cocktails and tapas as the sky shifts from blue to shades of mauve, pink and red over the Mediterranean. Venues such as Varadero are a benchmark of Valencian tardeo by the sea.

blocks.title: Tips for making the most of the Paseo Marítimo
items: The best way to get there from the centre is by bike along the Turia Gardens: 9 km of linear park without traffic lights all the way to the sea, the prettiest route in Valencia
For Sunday paella always book at the Paseo Neptuno restaurants: they are the most popular and without a reservation it is almost impossible to find a table in summer
The Paseo Marítimo at dawn is magical: the fishermen head out to sea, the promenade is empty and the Mediterranean light of daybreak on the water is impossible to photograph badly
La Patacona beach (Alboraya) is the quietest of the three: if you are looking for space and a local atmosphere rather than mass tourism, it is the best option, especially in August
In summer there are free yoga, Pilates and fitness classes on the sand: check the Valencia City Council’s “Sport and Health” programme for times
Tardeo on the Paseo Marítimo at sunset — they say the light takes on mauve and pink tones over the sea — is one of Valencians’ favourite weekend plans
